items.title: Custom skills, agents, and MCP servers in usage metrics API
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Copilot usage metrics now show the names of the skills, custom agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, slash commands, and plugins that your organization creates, instead of grouping them under other or custom. This builds on the agentic CLI customization metrics released in September. What’s new Named entries: In enterprise and organization reports, including per-user 1-day and 28-day reports, aggregated 1-day reports, and day_totals in aggregated 28-day reports, the totals_by_skill, totals_by_custom_agent, totals_by_mcp, totals_by_slash_cmd, and totals_by_plugin arrays now show the configured name of a customer-defined item instead of other or custom. More entries: Each totals_by_* list now includes up to 25 entries per record, up from five, so you can see more of the long tail of customizations your developers use. Any remaining activity is combined into a trailing other entry. Unchanged counts: interaction_count and the distinct_*_use_count fields are calculated the same way as before. Why this matters The customizations that matter most to an organization are often the ones its own teams build. Administrators can now see which internal skills, custom agents, and MCP servers developers actually use, track adoption after rolling out a new one, and focus enablement where it is needed. Important notes Coverage: Names are reported from Copilot CLI (interactive sessions and prompt mode), the GitHub Copilot app, Agent Client Protocol (ACP) integrations such as JetBrains, and the Copilot SDK. Prompt mode, the app, and ACP integrations require Copilot CLI 1.0.97 or later. The Copilot SDK requires v1.0.21 or later. IDEs report names when their agent experiences run on the Copilot SDK v1.0.21 or later. Names aren’t reported from an IDE’s built-in chat telemetry. Configured names: Names are reported as they are configured, trimmed and limited to 128 characters. Names that look like file paths stay grouped under other or custom. Review names before sharing reports out
items.why_it_matters: Copilot usage metrics now name the custom skills, agents and MCP servers in use. This helps fractional CTOs measure agentic tooling adoption at client organizations that use Copilot.

items.title: GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio — September update
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: September 2026 brought deeper visibility into your work: explore pull requests without leaving chat, bring the AI model your team trusts, and fix vulnerable packages the moment Visual Studio flags them. Highlights Here’s what’s new with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio 2026. Check the Insiders channel for the latest: Explore pull requests with the Git agent: The Git agent can now explore a pull request for you. Open GitHub Copilot Chat, select the Git agent, and attach a pull request as context from the Git Repository window to get a summary with navigable links to the underlying comments and files. This functionality requires connecting your Git provider’s MCP servers; GitHub and Azure DevOps are both supported. Updates to Bring Your Own Model (BYOM): BYOM is available in preview and lets you use the models your team prefers, through GitHub Copilot or your own model deployments, whether or not you’re signed in to GitHub. This feature is on by default across the Community, Professional, and Enterprise editions. Breaking change: BYOM now requires the new Agent (Preview), built on the GitHub Copilot SDK-powered harness. The previous Ask and Agent modes no longer support BYOM, and you’ll need to re-add previously configured Ollama models after updating. Supported providers include Microsoft Foundry, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama. Fix NuGet Vulnerabilities from the Error List: NuGet Audit warnings in the Error List now include a fixer action that opens GitHub Copilot Chat in agent mode and asks Copilot to fix the vulnerable packages using the NuGet MCP server. This functionality requires signing in to GitHub Copilot and enabling the NuGet MCP server from the Copilot Chat tools menu. This update is available to users on all GitHub Copilot plans, including Copilot Free, Student, Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise. Download Visual Studio 2026 to experience all the new Copilot features today. To learn more about what’s new, check out the Visual Studio blog and release
items.why_it_matters: Copilot updates for Visual Studio: PR exploration, bring-your-own model and vulnerable package fixes. Our team rarely uses Visual Studio, but it is useful context when advising clients on AI tooling.

items.title: EMU deletions fix
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Between June 1 and June 13, 2026, some Enterprise Managed User accounts that were deprovisioned through SCIM were incorrectly deleted instead of being suspended and obfuscated as expected. As a result, affected users appeared as ghost users in issues, pull requests, and audit logs, rather than retaining their expected suspended and obfuscated user records within the enterprise. Who was affected This affected approximately 12,285 Enterprise Managed User accounts across multiple enterprises. Most affected accounts had already been suspended and hard-deprovisioned, which means they couldn’t be reprovisioned by design. A smaller group of 76 accounts were active at the time of deletion. How to tell if you were affected You were affected if your enterprise audit logs contain a user.delete event for an Enterprise Managed User account during the June 1 to June 13, 2026 window. If you do not see any such events in that window, your enterprise was not impacted. If you do see these events, no action is required from you. GitHub is restoring the affected accounts. What caused the issue On June 1, 2026, GitHub enabled a change that routed deprovisioning requests through a new path. That path didn’t correctly check whether the account was an Enterprise Managed User account, which caused the affected accounts to be deleted instead of following the expected suspend-and-obfuscate flow. GitHub contained the issue by disabling the affected path on June 13, 2026. What we’re doing to fix it We’ve made code changes to prevent this from happening again. We’ve also restored affected user records in October 2026. The restoration process returned affected accounts to their expected suspended and obfuscated state, preserving traceability and audit history within the enterprise. Enterprise owners don’t need to take any action. Hard-deprovisioned Enterprise Managed User accounts can’t be reprovisioned by design, so this issue doesn’t affect the reprovisioning workflow. items.title: Enterprise installations for GitHub Apps generally available

You can replace classic PATs with GitHub Apps in more of your enterprise and organization automation with the expanded API support detailed below. These new and expanded permissions are focused on governance, security, and administrative settings for your enterprise, with two gaps at the organization level also closed. What’s new for GitHub Apps Governance: Manage enterprise-level repository policies and rulesets as well as read delegated bypass requests. Security: Configure two-factor authentication requirements, verify domains, manage IP allowlists, and control enterprise access restrictions. Administration: Update enterprise profiles and manage both member privileges and repository access settings across the enterprise. New permissions and API coverage Choose the permissions your workflow needs in your GitHub App settings. Permission Access Newly supported APIs and GraphQL data Enterprise organization and repository policies Read/write Read policy fields on EnterpriseOwnerInfo. Update private repository forking, default repository permissions, repository visibility changes, repository creation, repository deletion, issue deletion, collaborator invitations, deploy keys, protected branch updates, dependency insights setting, organization projects setting, and repository projects. Enterprise bypass requests Read Read push-rule and repository-policy bypass requests. Enterprise settings Read/write Read enterprise data through EnterpriseOwnerInfo, including server installations and organization invitations. Update the enterprise profile. Read is required for access to the enterprise organization and repository policies. Enterprise two-factor authentication Read/write Read two-factor fields on EnterpriseOwnerInfo. Update two-factor requirements and disallowed authentication methods. Enterprise verifiable domains; organization verifiable domains Write Access VerifiableDomains for enterprises or organiz

items.title: Turn notifications into code with the GitHub app in Teams
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: The new GitHub app in Teams brings notifications and copilot together, helping teams turn issues into fixes and ship code faster without leaving the conversation. Get notified in channels, group chats, or private chats, then @mention GitHub to turn updates into action. Turn an issue notification into a pull request Get notified: A bug report arrives in Teams. Take action: @GitHub investigates the issue, fixes the bug, and creates a pull request. Review and ship: Your team reviews, tests, and merges the fi Get started Explore the new GitHub app in Microsoft Teams, previously called GitHub notifications. If you already have GitHub notifications installed, update the app to the latest version. Your existing notification capabilities will continue to work. If you use the legacy GitHub app, which will be renamed “GitHub (deprecated)” and retired on November 16, install the consolidated GitHub app using the link above to continue using Copilot in Teams. In the consolidated app, mention @GitHub and follow any prompts to connect your GitHub account and select a repository. Join the discussion within the GitHub Community. The post Turn notifications into code with the GitHub app in Teams appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: The GitHub app in Teams lets Copilot turn issue notifications into PRs, relevant for clients on Microsoft Teams and for agent-driven issue-to-PR workflows.

items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.excerpt: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. This is max: For comparison, I ran fresh pelicans against Kimi K3 on those three reasoning levels. Via Hacker News Tags: ai, generative-ai, llms, llm, llm-pricing, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, llm-release, ai-in-china, moonshot, kimi
items.why_it_matters: Kimi K3.1 Pro claims parity with Opus 5.5 at half the price, with open weights promised by Nov 4. A meaningful cost and self-hosting option for client LLM features.
